# Higher-form symmetries

Lecture 27 · [Original notes](https://www.alucasphys.com/p7810s2026/p7810s2026_lecture27.pdf)

::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives"}
Derive subdiffusion from dipole conservation; construct subsystem-conserving dynamics; distinguish vector densities from scalar charges; interpret antisymmetric currents and higher-form charges geometrically; obtain the transverse diffusion mode of a one-form charge.
:::

## More conservation laws mean fewer allowed gradients {#sec-l27-response}

For an ordinary conserved density $n$, the response-field action has a constant-shift invariance $\pi\mapsto\pi+c$. Varying this transformation connects it to conservation of $Q=\int n$. More generally, a time-independent shift $\pi\mapsto\pi+f(\mathbf x)$ implies conservation of the weighted quantity

$$
Q_f=\int d^dx\,f(\mathbf x)n(\mathbf x).
$$ {#eq-l27-weighted}

Indeed, the change of the response kinetic term is $\int f\partial_tn=dQ_f/dt$; all other terms must be invariant or boundary terms. Boundary conditions are part of this statement. A formally conserved bulk moment can be changed by flux through the boundary.

This response-field viewpoint makes unfamiliar conservation laws easy to translate into a derivative expansion. The smallest allowed derivative acting on $\pi$ determines the slowest permitted relaxation process. It also unifies examples that are not all higher-form symmetries: dipole conservation and subsystem conservation generally refer to position-dependent scalar charges, whereas higher-form symmetries have a distinct geometric organization.

## Dipole-conserving matter {#sec-l27-dipole}

Suppose both total charge and all dipole moments are conserved:

$$
Q=\int n,\qquad D_i=\int x_i n.
$$

The response shifts are $\pi\mapsto\pi+a+b_ix_i$, so $\partial_i\pi$ is not invariant but $\partial_i\partial_j\pi$ is. With dimensionless thermodynamic potential $\mu=\delta\Phi/\delta n=n/\chi$, a simple isotropic action is

$$
\mathcal L=\pi\partial_tn
+iB(\partial_i\partial_j\pi)
\partial_i\partial_j(\pi-i\mu),\qquad B\ge0.
$$ {#eq-l27-dipole-action}

Temperature factors can be restored by taking $\Phi=F/T$ and matching the noise normalization. Varying $\pi$ and setting the response field to zero gives

$$
\partial_tn+B\nabla^4\mu=0,
\qquad\omega=-iD_4k^4,\qquad D_4=B/\chi.
$$ {#eq-l27-subdiffusion}

The sign follows from integrating by parts twice: the deterministic term is $+B\pi\nabla^4\mu$. The relaxation time scales as length to the fourth power, slower than ordinary diffusion's length squared. This is subdiffusion with dynamic exponent $z=4$ in this linear model.

A microscopic illustration is a one-dimensional lattice of occupations $n_x$ with allowed local rearrangements preserving both $\sum_xn_x$ and $\sum_xxn_x$. An isolated charge cannot hop one site without changing dipole moment; correlated moves can. Such constraints occur in fracton-inspired dynamics. The continuum equation predicts the long-wavelength relaxation when local equilibration and an ergodic hydrodynamic regime exist. Some microscopic models can have additional disconnected sectors, so observing $z=4$ requires checking that those do not invalidate the simple closure.

## Subsystem conservation {#sec-l27-subsystem}

On a square lattice one may instead conserve the charge on every row and every column. In the continuum, $\int dy\,n(x,y)$ is conserved for each $x$, and $\int dx\,n(x,y)$ is conserved for each $y$. Equivalently, $Q_{f,g}=\int dxdy\,[f(x)+g(y)]n$ is conserved for arbitrary functions $f,g$.

The response shift is $\pi\mapsto\pi+f(x)+g(y)$. Its simplest invariant derivative is $\partial_x\partial_y\pi$, giving

$$
\mathcal L=\pi\partial_tn
+iB_s(\partial_x\partial_y\pi)
\partial_x\partial_y(\pi-i\mu),
$$

and hence

$$
\omega=-iD_sk_x^2k_y^2,\qquad D_s=B_s/\chi.
$$ {#eq-l27-subsystem-dispersion}

Unlike $k^4$, this dispersion is not rotationally invariant. A fluctuation depending on only $x$ or only $y$ is frozen because it changes an exactly conserved row or column profile. The special axes are a physical remnant of the lattice, rather than a defect in the continuum approximation.

## A conserved quantity with a spatial index {#sec-l27-vector}

Now let the density itself be a vector, $b_i$. Before adding extra constraints, an isotropic first-derivative response theory can distinguish three irreducible pieces of $\partial_i\pi_j$: its trace, symmetric traceless part, and antisymmetric part. Write

$$
M_0=\partial_i\pi_i,\quad
M^{(2)}_{ij}=\frac{\partial_i\pi_j+\partial_j\pi_i}{2}
-\frac{\delta_{ij}}d\partial_k\pi_k,\quad
M^{(1)}_{ij}=\frac{\partial_i\pi_j-\partial_j\pi_i}{2}.
$$

A quadratic action can contain $i\sigma_aM_a(\pi)M_a(\pi-i\mu)$ for each sector, with nonnegative dissipative weights after fixing normalization. Selecting only one sector enlarges its shift symmetry and introduces more conserved quantities.

If only the trace term is present, divergence-free shifts of $\boldsymbol\pi$ are allowed. In three dimensions these can be represented locally by $\nabla\times\boldsymbol\Lambda$. The resulting conserved observables include circulation integrals $\oint_\gamma\mathbf b\cdot d\mathbf l$; the deterministic evolution of $\mathbf b$ is a gradient, which cannot change a closed-loop circulation. The lecture illustrates the corresponding singular test field using the Biot–Savart construction.

If only the antisymmetric sector is present, gradient shifts $\pi_i\mapsto\pi_i+\partial_i\Lambda$ are allowed instead. The local conservation of $\nabla\cdot\mathbf b$ follows. Integrating against a step-function $\Lambda$ turns this into conservation of flux through the boundary of a spatial region. This is the setting that leads naturally to a one-form current.

## The geometry of a higher-form current {#sec-l27-forms}

An ordinary symmetry has a vector current $J^\mu$ obeying $\partial_\mu J^\mu=0$. A continuous $p$-form symmetry has a totally antisymmetric current of rank $p+1$:

$$
\partial_{\mu_0}J^{\mu_0\mu_1\cdots\mu_p}=0.
$$ {#eq-l27-general-current}

In $d$ spatial dimensions its charge is integrated on a closed spatial submanifold of dimension $d-p$. “Closed” means no boundary; noncontractible cycles in periodic space are important examples. For $p=0$, this recovers the usual integral over all space. For $p=1$ in $d=3$, charge is a flux through a surface; for $p=2$, it is measured along a curve. This geometric definition is developed systematically in the primary reference [Gaiotto et al., *Generalized Global Symmetries*](https://doi.org/10.1007/JHEP02(2015)172).

For a one-form current, write $J^{0i}=b_i$ and $J^{ji}=K_{ji}=-K_{ij}$. Its spatial equation is

$$
\partial_tb_i+\partial_jK_{ji}=0.
$$ {#eq-l27-one-form}

The spatial equation alone implies $\partial_t(\partial_ib_i)=0$. The temporal-index component of the full source-free law @eq-l27-general-current additionally imposes $\partial_ib_i=0$. Thus an arbitrary frozen divergence is an extension with background charge, rather than the full source-free one-form conservation law. For the source-free theory, fluxes through homologous surfaces agree by Gauss's theorem. On an open surface the flux can change through its boundary; for magnetic flux this is Faraday's law. Thus higher-form conservation should not be misread as time independence of every open-surface flux.

For a two-form current in three spatial dimensions, dualize $J^{0ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}a_k$ and $J^{kij}=\epsilon_{kij}I$. The conservation equation becomes $\partial_t\mathbf a+\nabla I=0$ up to the chosen orientation convention. Integrating around any closed curve gives $d\oint\mathbf a\cdot d\mathbf l/dt=0$. This is the curve analogue of the surface-flux statement.

## Supplementary derivation: transverse diffusion {#sec-l27-modes}

Choose a quadratic equilibrium functional $\Phi=\int b_i b_i/(2\chi)$, so $\mu_i=b_i/\chi$. The antisymmetric response action gives a curl-type dissipative current, or equivalently

$$
\partial_tb_i=D(\nabla^2b_i-\partial_i\partial_jb_j),
\qquad D=\sigma/\chi\ge0.
$$ {#eq-l27-vector-diffusion}

For $\mathbf k=k\hat x$, the longitudinal component obeys $\partial_tb_x=0$, while each transverse component obeys $\partial_tb_\perp=-Dk^2b_\perp$. Thus

$$
\omega_\parallel=0,\qquad\omega_\perp=-iDk^2.
$$

The longitudinal zero mode records the static divergence sector of the extended spatial PDE. In the genuine source-free one-form theory, its temporal conservation equation requires $\nabla\cdot\mathbf b=0$, so the longitudinal mode is absent for nonzero $k$, leaving transverse diffusion. Notice the geometric wording: the polarization of the relaxing density is perpendicular to the wavevector. It does not mean the spatial modulation must be perpendicular to the density's original support.

Magnetic induction in a conductor is the immediate physical application: $\mathbf b=\mathbf B$, Gauss's law fixes the divergence-free sector, and finite resistivity produces this transverse diffusion. Coupling it to momentum introduces waves, the subject of the final lecture.

## Exercises and solutions {#sec-l27-exercises}

1. Check dipole conservation directly from @eq-l27-subdiffusion under decaying boundary conditions.
2. Identify every exactly frozen Fourier direction in @eq-l27-subsystem-dispersion.
3. Prove that @eq-l27-vector-diffusion preserves the initial divergence field.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
1. $\dot D_i=-D_4\int x_i\nabla^4n=0$ after moving the derivatives onto $x_i$ by integration by parts. The same calculation with $1$ verifies charge conservation.
2. All modes with $k_x=0$ or $k_y=0$ have zero decay rate. They encode the conserved row and column profiles.
3. Taking a divergence gives $\partial_t\partial_ib_i=D[\nabla^2\partial_ib_i-\nabla^2\partial_jb_j]=0$.
:::
